body: Two small words can join to make a compound word: sun + flower = sunflower.
A prefix goes at the start and changes meaning: un + happy = unhappy; re + do = redo. A suffix goes at the end: care + ful = careful; hope + less = hopeless.
Prefixes change a word: dis (not), mis (wrongly), pre (before), im/in (not), non (not), over, under, sub, mid.
Suffixes: ly, ness, ment, able, less, er. Exceptions: change y to i (happy, happiness) and le to ly (gentle, gently).
Some words do not follow the rules, so we learn them by heart: said, was, friend, because, people, would, they, where, again, school.
Homophones sound the same but are spelled differently: there / their / they're, to / too / two, hear / here, see / sea, right / write.

body: A statement tells (I like mangoes.). A question asks (Do you like mangoes?). A command tells someone what to do (Eat your mango.). An exclamation shows feeling (What a sweet mango!). Every sentence has a subject (who or what) and a predicate (what it does).

Many feminine words end in ة (taa marbuta). Examples: طالب (student, boy) → طالبة (student, girl); معلم → معلمة; مدرسة (school) is feminine.

Add ال (al) to a word to mean the: كتاب (a book) → الكتاب (the book). Before some letters, the ل is not pronounced: الشمس is read ash-shams. These are sun letters (ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن). The other 14 are moon letters, like القمر (al-qamar).
Arabic has singular, dual (two) and plural. كتاب (a book) → كتابان (two books) → كتب (books). ولد (boy) → أولاد (boys); بنت (girl) → بنات (girls). Many plurals change shape (broken plurals).
Arabic verbs have a base past form for he: كتب (kataba) he wrote, قرأ (qara'a) he read, ذهب (dhahaba) he went, أكل (akala) he ate, شرب (shariba) he drank, لعب (la'iba) he played.

t: Future, commands and what to say
body: Add س or سوف before the present verb for the future: سأكتب (sa-aktub) I will write. A command is short: اكتب! (uktub) write! اقرأ! (iqra') read! اجلس! (ijlis) sit!

لا (laa) = no / do not (present): لا أكتب (I do not write). لم (lam) + present = did not: لم أكتب (I did not write). ليس (laysa) = is not: الولد ليس كبيرا (the boy is not big). هل (hal) starts a yes/no question: هل أنت طالب؟ (Are you a student?)

The last vowel can change with the word's job. ـُ (u) for the doer: الولدُ. ـَ (a) for the thing acted on: رأيتُ الولدَ (I saw the boy). ـِ (i) after a preposition: في البيتِ (in the house). In everyday speech these endings are usually dropped.
